docs.title: Welcome to NebulaLE
docs.text:
NebulaLE (Nebula Low Energy) is a continuation of the Nebula simulator of electron-matter interaction, with specific focus on improving the simulator and its physics models to work better at low electron energies (< 100 eV).

The original Nebula simulator can be found on github, and its documentation is here. The basic functionality of the simulator has been explained there and will not be repeated here.

The main repository for NebulaLE can be found at: NebulaLE

The associated repository for cstoolLE is: cstoolLE.

docs.title: Known Bugs
docs.text: This is a list of known issues that are still in the Nebula or cstool code.

docs.title: Nebula:
docs.text:
• Energy deposition mode double counts SE energies, meaning that if you sum up the energy of all energy deposition events dE you get a number that is higher than the number of primaries \(\times\) the primary landing energy

  • Incorrectly sampled q values for inelastic scattering cause a very small number of scattering angle costheta values to be larger than 1. This is likely due to an interpolation error near 0 of the icdf table.

  • The trajectories function does not output all SE generation events, for some reason.

  • Setting the minimum simulation energy to a negative number in order to lower the simulation cutoff threshold energy results in an unexpectedly large number of 0 energy loss edep events

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
There are currently 5 commands one can run in order to use NebulaLE:

  • nebula_gpu

  • nebula_cpu_mt

  • nebula_cpu_edep

  • nebula_cpu_traj

  • nebula_cpu_SE_mode

docs.title: GPU version: nebula_gpu
docs.text: Run Nebula on the GPU. Not all changes in NebulaLE are guaranteed to work for GPU, so use of this version is not recommended.

docs.title: CPU main version: nebula_cpu_mt
docs.text: Run Nebula on the CPU. This is the standard version of Nebula.

docs.title: CPU edep version: nebula_cpu_edep
docs.text:
Run Nebula on the CPU, with a custom output datatype that logs energy deposition events. Detection events (if detector is present) are stored in a .bin file instead of a .det file.

The output datatype is given by:

import numpy as np

energy_dtype = np.dtype([ 
('x', '=f'), 
('y', '=f'), 
('z', '=f'), # Position 
('E', '=f'), # Energy of electron before collision at position x, y, z (in eV) 
('dE', '=f'), # Energy loss (deV) 
('px', '=i'), # Pixel x of initial primary beam electron 
('py', '=i')]) # Pixel y of initial primary beam electron

(Current bug: total energy outputted is too high: Secondary electron energy is double counted.)

docs.title: CPU trajectories version: nebula_cpu_traj
docs.text:
Run Nebula on the CPU, with a custom output datatype that logs every single event that the electron encounters (inelastic, elastic, boundary crossing (transmission and reflection), mirroring (against a mirror plane), detection, termination. IDs of each event type are custom, and require a special script to interpret.

The output datatype is given by:

import numpy as np

trajectory_dtype = np.dtype([ 
('x', '=f'), 
('y', '=f'), 
('z', '=f'), # Position 
('E', '=f'), # Energy of electron before collision at position x, y, z (in eV) 
('dE', '=f'), # Energy loss (deV) 
('px', '=i'), # Pixel x of initial primary beam electron 
('py', '=i'), # Pixel y of initial primary beam electron 
('tag', '=i'), # Unique ID tag of initial primary beam electron  
('ns', '=i')]) # Consecutive scattering event number

(Current bug: blocks GPU compilation, there seem to be some inelastic events missing in the list of output events.)

docs.title: CPU SE version: nebula_cpu_SE_mode
docs.text:
Run Nebula on the CPU, with an additional output of the scatter counter. This is distinct from the trajectories version because it focuses on detected electrons and not "events" in general.

The output datatype is given by:

import numpy as np

SE_mode_dtype = np.dtype([ 
('x', '=f'), 
('y', '=f'), 
('z', '=f'), # Position 
('dx', '=f'), 
('dy', '=f'), 
('dz', '=f'), # Direction 
('E', '=f'), # Energy 
('sc', '=i'), # Scatter counter 
('px', '=i'), 
('py', '=i')]) # Pixel index

(Current bug: blocks GPU compilation)

docs.title: CstoolLE version 1.0.7
docs.text: Identical to the latest version of cstool (2024-08-21), at link: cstool

docs.title: Added minimum excitation to .mat file
docs.text:
The minimum excitation for metals is the Fermi level from the bottom of the valence band and for insulators and semiconductors it is the valence band width plus the band gap.

We need this quantity in Nebula because the omega axis for the q_2dicdf (in other words the q icdf table) output from cstool is written between the lowest optical excitation energy (~0.01 eV) and \(E-E_{\min}\) where \(E_{\min}\) is the minimum excitation energy. However, since the omega axis has no scale output in cstool, Nebula reads it as a 0 to 1 scale, which changes the energy zero point from the valence band to the minimum excitation level, which is not the same energy reference as the rest of the simulator.

In short, \(E_\min\) is outputted here to be used in Nebula to read the table using \(\frac{\omega}{E-E\min}\) instead of \(\frac{\omega}{E}\)

docs.title: Separated phonon and Mott scattering
docs.text:
Mott and phonon scattering cross sections are usually merged using the Kieft and Bosch approach. This has been removed and the two models are separated and outputted. There is also functionality to write the pdf and cdfs to the .mat file if desired, but to save space it is disabled.

Note that because the old Kieft model is not written to .mat file by default now, this version of the .mat file requires NebulaLE version 1.1.0 or higher to run. One can of course change the separate bool to false in cstool.py to overcome this.

docs.title: CstoolLE version 1.1.1
docs.text:
pkg_resources was long deprecated, so the dependency was removed and replaced with a new one. This package was only used to identify and download the relevant endf files for ionization cross sections.

New implementation basically follows the migration guide exactly.

Note that endf files are saved not in cstool/data/endf_data, but where your virtual environment / python installation lives. This is because python treats the endf files as resources for the cstool package.

docs.title: NebulaLE version 1.0.3
docs.text: Identical to the latest version of Nebula (2021-05-24), at link: Nebula

docs.title: Fixed q reading off energy reference mismatch.
docs.text: The output omega axis for the q tables should run from the minimum optical excitation to \(E-E_{\min}\), where \(E_\min\) the minimum excitation energy. However, the table is outputted with no scale from cstool and so is read in Nebula as a 0 to 1 scale, thus changing the energy zero point from the valence band minimum to the minimum excitation level, which causes a misreading and q values to be sampled incorrectly. We change this reference in full_penn.h from \(\frac{\omega}{E}\) to \(\frac{\omega}{E-E\min}\).

docs.title: Separated phonon and Mott scattering
docs.text:
While Kieft and Bosch introduced the hybrid model which interpolates between phonon scattering and Mott scattering, we argue that the two are distinct scattering channels that are independent of each other and so should be selected between following Mathiessen's rule.

Requires a .mat file from cstool version 1.1.0 or later to run.
